questions.prompt: Which OpenIddict endpoint automatically generates and exposes the public keys your API uses for validation?
questions.explanation: The Authorization Endpoint handles login and consent, the Token Endpoint validates client requests and issues JWTs, and the JWKS Endpoint publishes the public keys.

questions.prompt: With OpenIddict, what is left for your code to do when creating a JWT?
options: Choose the algorithm, sign the token and serialise it
Create the `ClaimsPrincipal`; OpenIddict generates the JWT from it
Nothing; OpenIddict also decides which claims the user has
Write the token endpoint's HTTP handling by hand
questions.explanation: Without OpenIddict you handle claims, signing, expiry, algorithm, issuer, audience and serialisation yourself. With it you create the `ClaimsPrincipal` and OpenIddict produces the JWT.

questions.prompt: A request with `Authorization: Bearer eyJ...` reaches `GET /api/orders`. Put what the API does in order.
steps: Validate the JWT's signature, issuer, audience and expiration
questions.explanation: The API doesn't ask OpenIddict about every request; once it has the signing keys, validation is local and fast.

source.section: Why This Matters for Your API

questions.prompt: Does every app or website with login and registration need a separate auth server?
options: Yes, issuing your own JWTs from a Web API is never done in production
Yes, because refresh tokens only work with a separate auth server
No, but only if the app has no refresh tokens
No, a `/login` endpoint in your own Web API is normal for a single application and team
questions.explanation: Login inside your own Web API is used by many production systems, typically one frontend plus one backend with nothing else sharing the identity.

source.section: Option A: No separate auth server (login lives in your own WebAPI)

questions.prompt: A calendar app built by an outside developer wants permission to read a user's tasks on your platform. Which reason for a separate authorization server does this match?
options: Third-party applications need access to your APIs, the primary use case OAuth 2.0 was designed for
Single sign-on across your own products
You don't want to maintain password hashing code
questions.explanation: The authorization server obtains the user's consent and issues an access token with limited scopes, so the third-party app never sees the password and access can be revoked.

source.section: 4. Third-Party Applications Need Access to Your APIs
